prompt: On a Wi-Fi network, who decides when a laptop moves from one access point to another?
hint: It is not like a mobile phone network.

choices.text: The access point it is on
choices.why: The AP at most suggests, with 802.11v; it cannot move the client.

choices.text: The controller, from the signal the APs report
choices.why: A controller sees the signal and still only suggests or disconnects; the move is the client's.

choices.text: The laptop, by its own algorithm
choices.why: Right. Its operating system or driver decides, with a threshold the standard does not fix.

choices.text: The RADIUS server, when it reauthenticates
choices.why: RADIUS answers whether a person may join, not which AP they use.

prompt: One sticky laptop sits at a low data rate on AP A. Why do the other ten clients on AP A get slower?
hint: A channel carries one transmission at a time.

choices.text: The AP lowers every client's rate to match it
choices.why: Each client keeps its own rate; the harm is in the time, not the rate.

choices.text: Its slow transmissions occupy the channel for longer
choices.why: Right. The same data at a low rate takes more airtime, and nobody else transmits meanwhile.

choices.text: It uses up the AP's limit on associated clients
choices.why: One client more is nowhere near the association limit.

choices.text: Its retransmissions go to AP B and interfere there
choices.why: It is associated to A, and its frames go to A.

prompt: Why does switching off the 1, 2, 5.5 and 11 Mbit/s rates on a 2.4 GHz network help clients roam?
hint: Where does a cell end?

choices.text: It makes every client transmit faster, so roams take less time
choices.why: The roam itself is not shortened; its trigger moves.

choices.text: It forces clients onto 5 GHz
choices.why: That is band steering, a different mechanism.

choices.text: It turns on 802.11k neighbour reports
choices.why: Neighbour reports are their own setting, unrelated to data rates.

choices.text: It shrinks each cell's edge, so the client's threshold comes sooner
choices.why: Right. The slow rates were what kept a distant client associated.

prompt: A client that stays on a distant access point after a better one is available is called a ___ client.
hint: It clings.

prompt: Match each amendment to what it adds to a roam.
hint: Finding, deciding, keys.

pairs.right: A list of nearby APs and their channels
A suggestion from the AP to move elsewhere
Keys prepared in advance for the next AP

prompt: An AP sends a client an 802.11v BSS transition request pointing at a better AP. What happens next?
hint: It is a request.

choices.text: The client is moved to the named AP
choices.why: Nothing in 802.11 moves a client against its will.

choices.text: It accepts or declines
choices.why: Right. 802.11v is an offer, and a client without it ignores it.

choices.text: The controller disconnects the client
choices.why: Disconnecting is a separate, blunter tool.

choices.text: The two APs exchange the client's keys
choices.why: Key preparation is 802.11r's job, not 802.11v's.

prompt: On an 802.1X network with 802.11r, what does a client skip when it moves to a new AP in the same mobility domain?
hint: The slowest step of the three.

choices.text: The association with the new AP
choices.why: It still joins; the keys ride inside the join frames.

choices.text: Encryption, until the next full login
choices.why: Traffic is encrypted from the first frame after the roam.

choices.text: A new EAP exchange with the RADIUS server
choices.why: Right. The key for the new AP was derived from the first authentication.

choices.text: The scan of the other channels
choices.why: Cutting the scan is 802.11k's contribution.

prompt: Put the steps of a roam without 802.11k, v or r in order.
hint: Find, join, keys.
items: The signal of the current AP falls below the client's threshold
The client scans the other channels
Authentication and reassociation with the new AP
The four-way handshake with the new AP
trap: Keys come last: they are negotiated with the AP the client has just joined.

prompt: After 802.11r is switched on, a batch of old barcode scanners can no longer join the SSID at all. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What changed is what the AP advertises.

choices.text: Their drivers fail on an SSID that advertises FT
choices.why: Right. A mixed mode, or a separate SSID for them, and a test with the real devices.

choices.text: 802.11r needs a new passphrase
choices.why: FT keeps the same authentication; only the key hierarchy is added.

choices.text: The RADIUS server rejects devices without certificates
choices.why: Nothing about the RADIUS policy changed.

choices.text: 802.11r works on 5 GHz alone
choices.why: FT is not tied to a band.

prompt: On which UDP port does CAPWAP's control channel run?
hint: Data is the next one up.

prompt: A controller that tunnels all users' traffic loses power and has no pair. What happens to the clients?
hint: Where does their traffic join the wired network?

choices.text: Nothing, since the APs keep beaconing
choices.why: Beacons are not traffic; the tunnel's far end is gone.

choices.text: They lose the network until it returns
choices.why: Right. That is why controllers run in pairs.

choices.text: They fall back to their last autonomous configuration
choices.why: Lightweight APs are not autonomous APs waiting in reserve.

choices.text: They lose encryption but keep working
choices.why: Nothing falls back to plain text; the path is simply gone.

prompt: In a split-MAC design, which of these stays in the access point rather than moving to the controller?
hint: What has to happen within microseconds?

choices.text: Choosing the channel plan
choices.why: The controller does that, seeing every AP at once.

choices.text: Deciding which clients may associate
choices.why: Association can wait milliseconds and goes to the controller.

choices.text: Holding the keys for roaming
choices.why: Sharing keys between APs is one reason for a controller.

choices.text: Acknowledging each received frame
choices.why: Right. An acknowledgement has microseconds to go out, so it stays in the AP.

prompt: A shop's cloud-managed APs lose their internet link for an hour. What is the usual consequence in the designs described?
hint: Management and data take different paths.

choices.text: Every client is disconnected until the link returns
choices.why: The data stays on site; the APs keep their last configuration.

choices.text: Clients keep working; configuration is frozen
choices.why: Right, and anything hosted in the cloud, such as a portal, stops too.

choices.text: The APs switch to open authentication
choices.why: Security settings do not change when management is unreachable.

choices.text: The APs elect one of themselves as controller
choices.why: That is a feature of some products, not what cloud management means.

prompt: A client at 400 Mbit/s sends 10 MB in 0.2 s of airtime. How many seconds does the same 10 MB take at 25 Mbit/s, ignoring overhead?
hint: 80 million bits.

prompt: A data sheet says an AP supports 500 clients. What does that number describe?
hint: Associated is not the same as served.

choices.text: How many can stream video at once
choices.why: Airtime runs out long before that.

choices.text: How many a typical office should put on it
choices.why: Planning figures are a few dozen active clients per radio.

choices.text: How many it will keep associated
choices.why: Right. A table size, not a capacity.

choices.text: The total across both of its radios' channels at full rate
choices.why: Rate and client count are different axes; the number is a count of associations.

prompt: A lecture theatre with 200 laptops is slow. Which of these add capacity? Choose all that apply.
hint: Airtime per channel is fixed; channels and good rates are not.

choices.text: More APs on different channels, each at lower power
choices.why: Right. Each channel is another stream of airtime, and lower power keeps the cells small.

choices.text: Raising every AP's transmit power
choices.why: Bigger cells hear each other and share airtime; lesson 7 turns power down.

choices.text: Steering dual-band laptops to 5 GHz
choices.why: Right. 5 GHz has more channels to spread them over.

choices.text: Switching off the lowest data rates
choices.why: Right. No client holds the channel at 1 Mbit/s any more.

choices.text: Adding a second SSID for half the room
choices.why: Same channel, same airtime, and more beacons in it.

prompt: Why do two vendors' band steering features behave differently on the same clients?
hint: Look for it in the standard.

choices.text: Each is a certified 802.11 profile with options
choices.why: There is no 802.11 band steering profile to certify.

choices.text: It is not standardised; each vendor wrote its own
choices.why: Right. Some delay probe responses, some use 802.11v, and the tuning differs.

choices.text: It depends on the country code of each AP
choices.why: The country code sets channels and power, not steering.

choices.text: The clients choose which vendor to obey
choices.why: Clients do not know which feature is at work; they see its effects.

prompt: A new Wi-Fi 6 AP is plugged into an 802.3af port. It boots and serves clients, but capacity is lower than designed. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: 15.4 W at the port, 12.95 W at the device.

choices.text: 802.3af limits the data rate of the Ethernet link
choices.why: PoE sets power, not the link speed.

choices.text: The AP is sticky to its first client
choices.why: Stickiness is a client behaviour, not an AP one.

choices.text: It turned a radio or streams off
choices.why: Right. It says so in a log line, and the switch's PoE status shows the class it got.

choices.text: The switch is over its PoE budget
choices.why: Then the port would be refused power, not powered at 802.3af.

prompt: A switch has a PoE budget of 740 W and reserves by class. It already powers 10 cameras at 15.4 W each. How many 802.3at APs, reserved at 30 W each, fit beside them?
hint: Take the cameras off first, then divide and round down.

prompt: A floor's twelve APs all fit on one switch's PoE budget. Why split them across two switches anyway?
hint: What happens when that switch fails?

choices.text: PoE works better on shorter cable runs
choices.why: Cable length is within the standard either way; the point is failure.

choices.text: A dead switch then leaves half the cells up
choices.why: Right. Alternating neighbours makes a failure patchy coverage rather than none.

choices.text: Each switch can then run a different SSID
choices.why: SSIDs are the APs' configuration, not the switches'.

choices.text: A controller requires two uplinks per floor
choices.why: No controller requires that; the reason is the switch as a single point of failure.

prompt: A hospital's voice handsets on WPA2-Enterprise drop a second of audio whenever a nurse walks between wards. Which change goes at the cause?
hint: Where does a roam spend its time on 802.1X?

choices.text: Raising the APs' power so the handsets roam less
choices.why: Bigger cells defer the roam and make it no faster; they add sticky zones.

choices.text: Moving the handsets to WPA3-Personal
choices.why: That loses per-person credentials to save the EAP exchange; 802.11r saves it and keeps them.

choices.text: 802.11r, tested with those handsets
choices.why: Right. The full EAP exchange on every roam is the cost, and fast transition removes it.

choices.text: Band steering the handsets to 2.4 GHz
choices.why: The band does not change the key exchange a roam performs.

prompt: A chain of 40 small shops has two APs each and no IT staff on site. Which architecture fits best?
hint: 80 APs, 40 places, one team.

choices.text: Autonomous APs, configured one by one
choices.why: Eighty separate logins for every change, and nobody on site to help.

choices.text: A controller in each shop
choices.why: Forty controllers to buy, run and pair for two APs each.

choices.text: Cloud-managed APs
choices.why: Right. One screen for all 40 sites, no box on site, and the shops' traffic stays local.

choices.text: One central controller tunnelling all traffic to head office
choices.why: Every shop's traffic would cross the WAN and stop when that link or controller fails.

prompt: Put the steps of planning a room's Wi-Fi capacity in order.
hint: Start from the clients, end at the radios.
items: Count the devices active at once
Divide by what one radio really delivers
Place that many radios on different channels
trap: The number of radios is the answer, so it comes last; the data sheet's client count is not an input.
